title: Cymbeline
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Cymbeline's Britain under Roman tribute, Philario's house in Rome, and the mountains above Milford Haven
lengthNote: Around 3,300 lines across twenty-nine scenes, which move between a British court, a house in Rome and a cave in Wales
openingLine: You do not meet a man but frowns
summary: Cymbeline's daughter Imogen has married a poor gentleman, Posthumus, and her father has banished him. In Rome a stranger named Iachimo bets that he can seduce her, fails, hides in a trunk in her bedroom, and comes away with enough true detail to pass as proof. What follows is a princess walking across Britain in boy's clothes, two lost princes keeping house in a Welsh cave, a Roman invasion, and a last scene that unties every knot in front of the whole cast at once.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation here is taken word for word from this text, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, from which modern editions vary by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Simon Forman saw it before he died in September 1611, which is the latest it can have reached the stage.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives. The First Folio prints it last among the tragedies, at the very end of the volume.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: British kings and the Roman tribute from the Chronicles; the wager on a wife from the ninth tale of the Decameron's second day.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: More changes of place than anything else in the Folio: court, Rome, a mountain cave, a battlefield, a prison, a tent.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A marriage the king will not have
structure.summary: Two gentlemen tell the audience what the court cannot say aloud: the princess has married a poor gentleman, the king has banished him, and every courtier is privately glad. Imogen and Posthumus exchange a ring and a bracelet before he sails. Within a single evening at Philario's table in Rome, a stranger has turned that marriage into a bet, and by the end of the act he has talked his way into her bedroom with a trunk.

scenes.title: The two gentlemen
scenes.summary: A courtier lays out the marriage, the banishment, and the two royal sons stolen from the nursery twenty years ago and never traced.

scenes.title: The ring and the bracelet
scenes.summary: Imogen and Posthumus part under the Queen's eye and exchange two gifts that the rest of the play will use as evidence. Cymbeline arrives and drives him out.

scenes.title: Cloten, and the ship growing small
scenes.summary: Cloten swaggers about a duel he lost while two lords mock him in asides. Imogen makes Pisanio describe her husband's departure until the ship is the size of a gnat.

scenes.title: The wager at Philario's
scenes.summary: Iachimo needles Posthumus into staking Imogen's diamond on her fidelity. Philario tries to stop it; the terms are drawn up by lawyers instead.

scenes.title: Poison, and a trunk
scenes.summary: The Queen collects drugs from her doctor and plants a box on Pisanio. Iachimo tries Imogen directly, is thrown out, apologises handsomely, and asks her to keep a trunk of plate in her bedchamber overnight.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Proof made out of true details
structure.summary: Iachimo climbs out of the trunk at midnight, writes down the pictures, the chimneypiece and the andirons, slips the bracelet off Imogen's arm and notes the mole on her breast. In Rome every item he recites is correct, and Posthumus believes the one thing that is not. Between the two scenes Cloten wakes Imogen with hired musicians and is told that his rival's oldest coat is worth more than the whole of him.

scenes.title: Cloten at bowls
scenes.summary: Two lords flatter Cloten to his face and insult him in asides. Left alone, one of them prays that Imogen's honour will hold.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: Iachimo leaves the trunk, inventories the room, takes the bracelet, finds the mole, and notices she fell asleep over the tale of Tereus.

scenes.title: Hark, hark! the lark
scenes.summary: Cloten hires music to wake her, and Imogen tells him Posthumus's meanest garment is dearer to her than every hair on his head.

scenes.title: The reckoning in Rome
scenes.summary: Iachimo describes the tapestry, the chimneypiece and the andirons, produces the bracelet, then names the mole. Posthumus hands over the diamond.

scenes.title: The woman's part
scenes.summary: Alone, Posthumus decides every vice in man is inherited from his mother, and resolves to write against women for the rest of his life.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Two letters, and the road to Milford
structure.summary: Britain refuses the Roman tribute in the same hours that two letters from Posthumus reach the court: one telling Imogen to meet him at Milford Haven, one telling Pisanio to kill her when she gets there. Pisanio shows her the second, refuses to use his sword, and dresses her as a boy. In the mountains above the haven an exiled lord is raising two young men who do not know they are the king's sons.

scenes.title: No more tribute
scenes.summary: Lucius asks for the three thousand pounds a year Cassibelan granted. The Queen and Cloten talk Cymbeline into refusing, and Rome declares war.

scenes.title: The two letters
scenes.summary: Pisanio reads his order to commit murder, hides it, and hands Imogen the letter that sends her galloping for Wales.

scenes.title: The cave
scenes.summary: Belarius takes his boys hunting past a door so low it bows them, then tells the audience who they are and why he stole them.

scenes.title: Near Milford Haven
scenes.summary: Imogen reads the charge of adultery, offers Pisanio her heart and his sword, and is talked instead into the doublet and hose of Fidele.

scenes.title: Cloten takes the clothes
scenes.summary: Cloten wrings Posthumus's suit out of Pisanio and rides for Milford with rape in mind; Imogen, starving, walks into the cave and is made welcome; Rome levies gentlemen volunteers under Iachimo.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A grave dug for the wrong body
structure.summary: Guiderius kills Cloten in Posthumus's clothes and sends the head down the creek. Imogen swallows the Queen's drug, is laid out as dead, and is buried with a song by two brothers who think she is a boy called Fidele. She wakes beside a headless corpse in her husband's suit, reads it as her husband, and is picked up by the Roman general as his page.

scenes.title: Cloten admires himself
scenes.summary: Wearing Posthumus's suit, Cloten measures his own legs against his rival's and rehearses the murder and the rape he means to carry out in it.

scenes.title: Fear no more
scenes.summary: Cloten loses his head to Guiderius. Imogen is laid beside his body as dead, the brothers speak the dirge, and she wakes to the wrong conclusion.

scenes.title: The king with nobody left
scenes.summary: Cymbeline has lost his daughter, his stepson and his queen to a fever, and the legions have landed on his coast.

scenes.title: The boys go to the war
scenes.summary: Guiderius and Arviragus refuse to hide higher in the mountains, and Belarius gives way and follows them down to the British army.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: A battle, a god, and everything said out loud
structure.summary: Posthumus lands with the Roman army, changes out of his Italian clothes and fights for the country he believes he has widowed. An old man and two boys hold a narrow lane and turn the rout into a British victory. In prison Jupiter comes down on an eagle and leaves a riddle on the sleeper's chest. In Cymbeline's tent every disguise, lie and supposed death is unpicked in front of everybody.

scenes.title: The bloody cloth
scenes.summary: Holding the handkerchief he asked for as proof of the murder, Posthumus resolves to die in British clothes for the wife he had killed.

scenes.title: The battle
scenes.summary: Posthumus disarms Iachimo without either knowing the other; Belarius and the boys rescue a captured Cymbeline.

scenes.title: The narrow lane
scenes.summary: Posthumus tells a fleeing lord how two striplings and an old man turned the battle, loses his temper at him, and is taken prisoner as a Roman.

scenes.title: Jupiter on an eagle
scenes.summary: The ghosts of the Leonati circle the sleeping Posthumus and petition the god, who throws a thunderbolt, leaves a tablet on his chest and ascends.

scenes.title: In Cymbeline's tent
scenes.summary: The Queen's deathbed confession, Iachimo's confession, the ring, the page who is a wife, Cloten's head, the mole on a neck, and peace with Rome.

characters.name: Imogen
characters.role: Cymbeline's daughter and heir, married to Posthumus
characters.summary: She is the only person in the play who never mistakes anybody. She argues her father down in the second scene, refuses Cloten to his face, reads her own death warrant and hands over the sword herself, walks two days into Wales on her own feet, and cooks for the men who turn out to be her brothers. The play keeps burying her and she keeps getting up.
characters.clue: She reads herself to sleep over the tale of Tereus, and wakes on a hillside beside a headless man in her husband's suit.

relationships.label: stepdaughter of, and marked for poison by

characters.name: Posthumus Leonatus
characters.role: An orphan raised at Cymbeline's court, and Imogen's husband
characters.summary: Everyone praises him in the first scene, and by the middle of the second act he has done the worst thing in the play. He stakes his wife's fidelity on a bet with a man he met at dinner, believes a bracelet over everything he knows of her, and posts an order to cut her throat. The fifth act is given over to his repentance, and he opens it by asking to be hanged.
characters.clue: He gives a diamond away over supper and orders a murder by letter, then comes back to Britain dressed as a peasant to be killed.

relationships.label: ward of, banished by, son-in-law to
wears the same suit, to opposite ends

characters.name: Iachimo
characters.role: A Roman gentleman who bets he can seduce Imogen
characters.summary: He tries the direct route first, is thrown out of the room, and switches to a trunk. What makes him dangerous is that he never lies about a detail: the tapestry, the chimneypiece, the silver Cupids and the mole are all exactly as he says. He builds a falsehood entirely out of true statements, and by the last act he cannot stop confessing it.
characters.clue: He spends a night in a woman's bedroom without touching her and leaves with everything he needs to wreck her marriage.

relationships.label: assails, then robs while she sleeps

characters.name: Cymbeline
characters.summary: He banishes his son-in-law, loses his daughter, lets his wife run his foreign policy, and spends the middle of the play offstage being wrong about all three. His judgement is not so much restored as overtaken: the Queen dies confessing, his stolen sons walk back into the tent, and at the end he pays the tribute he went to war over, having won the war.
characters.clue: He fights Rome to stop paying three thousand pounds a year, beats them, and then offers to pay it.

characters.name: The Queen
characters.role: Cymbeline's second wife, and Cloten's mother
characters.summary: She keeps a doctor on hand for poisons, assures Imogen she is not the stepmother of the stories, and means to put her own son on the throne over her stepdaughter's body. Her speech on Britain's rocks and roaring waters is the most patriotic thing anybody says in the play. She dies raving, having confessed that she never loved her husband and married his crown.
characters.clue: She asks her physician for slow poisons and is quietly handed a sleeping draught instead, and never finds out.

characters.name: Cloten
characters.role: The Queen's son by her first husband, and Imogen's suitor
characters.summary: He is stupid, violent and obsessed with his own rank, and two lords insult him in asides for a whole scene without his noticing. He is also the engine of the worst thing that happens on stage: told that his rival's poorest coat is worth more than he is, he puts that coat on to commit a rape and a murder, and loses his head to a boy who has no idea who he is.
characters.clue: He hires musicians at dawn to penetrate a woman who despises him, and dies in another man's suit in a wood.

relationships.label: suitor to, then would-be rapist of
wears his clothes and dies in them

characters.name: Pisanio
characters.role: Posthumus's servant, left behind in Britain with Imogen
characters.summary: He is handed a letter ordering him to murder his mistress and works out, in the time it takes to read it, that obeying would be the dishonest thing. He shows her the letter, refuses the sword she offers him, invents Fidele, sends a bloody cloth to Rome as false proof of a death, and then holds his tongue through two acts of threat and torture.
characters.clue: He is given a poison box by the Queen and a murder order by his master, and turns both into ways of keeping Imogen alive.

relationships.label: servant of, and disobeys to keep faith

characters.name: Belarius
characters.role: A lord banished twenty years ago, living in Wales under the name Morgan
characters.summary: Two men swore he was in league with Rome, Cymbeline believed them, and he answered by carrying the king's infant sons out of the nursery. He has raised them well and knows it, and he spends the play watching an inherited nature break through the life he gave them. Handing them back in the last scene costs him the only family he has.
characters.clue: He answers to Morgan, keeps house in a cave with a door so low it bows whoever goes through it, and has had the heirs of Britain inside it for twenty years.

relationships.label: stole and raised as his son Polydore
stole and raised as his son Cadwal

characters.name: Guiderius
characters.role: Cymbeline's elder lost son, raised as Polydore
characters.summary: He is the blunt one. He tells Belarius the cave is a debtor's prison, declines to be impressed when Cloten announces he is the Queen's son, cuts his head off and throws it in the creek, and says at his own trial that he did it and is glad of it. He cannot sing, so he speaks his half of the dirge over a sister he does not recognise.
characters.clue: A mole shaped like a bloody star on his neck is what finally tells his father who he is.

relationships.label: son of, restored in the last scene

characters.name: Arviragus
characters.role: Cymbeline's younger lost son, raised as Cadwal
characters.summary: He is the one who talks about the flowers. Where his brother is short, he is lavish: he offers to bleed a whole parish of Clotens to bring the colour back to Fidele's cheek, and lists the pale primrose, the azured harebell and the leaf of eglantine he means to strew on the grave. He carries his sister's body on stage in his arms and is told off for wench-like words.
characters.clue: He promises to sweeten a grave with wild flowers all summer, and is cut short by his brother for playing with the wording.

relationships.label: son of, restored in the last scene

themes.name: What counts as proof
themes.summary: Iachimo's report is accurate in every particular and wrong in its conclusion. The bracelet was on her arm, the mole is under her breast, the andirons are two winking Cupids of silver, and none of it touches the question Posthumus actually asked.
themes.development: Objects carry the case in the first half and are overturned in the second, when a second mole, on Guiderius's neck, gives a father back his son.

themes.name: How fast belief turns
themes.summary: Posthumus goes from staking everything on his wife's honour to ordering her murder inside a single scene, and the turn happens on a bracelet he has already been told could have been stolen by a servant.
themes.development: Philario argues for doubt in 2.4 and is brushed aside; by the fifth act Posthumus is making the same case against himself and asking for a cord or a knife.

themes.name: Clothes, names and who people take you for
themes.summary: Imogen becomes Fidele, Belarius answers to Morgan, the princes are Polydore and Cadwal, Cloten dies in Posthumus's suit and Posthumus fights in a peasant's. Almost nobody in Wales is called by their own name.
themes.development: Disguise keeps people alive until Cloten borrows a suit, after which it starts killing them; the last scene works by taking every borrowed name back.

themes.name: What a servant owes
themes.summary: Pisanio is ordered to commit murder by a master he loves, and decides that keeping faith means refusing. The Queen tries to buy him with preferment, Cloten tries to frighten him with a drawn sword, and he goes on serving Imogen through both.
themes.development: Posthumus himself supplies the verdict in 5.1, saying that every good servant does not all commands; by then Pisanio has been proved right for two acts.

themes.name: Birth showing through
themes.summary: Two boys brought up in a cave stand and fight like princes the moment a battle reaches them, and Belarius says openly that he has never been able to hide it. The play insists that breeding will out, and that the cave has done them no harm at all.
themes.development: What starts as Belarius's private astonishment in 3.3 becomes state business in 5.5, when the succession he stole is handed back over a mantle and a mole.

themes.name: Britain, Rome and the tribute
themes.summary: Cymbeline refuses three thousand pounds a year and goes to war over it, egged on by a queen with her own reasons and a stepson who thinks Britain is a world by itself. Britain wins the battle and then agrees to pay anyway.
themes.development: Roman arrogance in 3.1 becomes Roman defeat in 5.2, and the settlement hands the money back without handing back the victory.

themes.name: Pardon's the word
themes.summary: Posthumus, standing over the man who destroyed his marriage, tells him the only power he has is to spare him. Cymbeline then pardons everybody in the tent, including the army he has just beaten and the boy who beheaded his stepson.
themes.development: The play withholds punishment from almost everyone. The two who die, Cloten and the Queen, are the two who never ask for anything.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: A ring, a bracelet and a box travel the length of the play. The bracelet comes off Imogen's arm in the dark in 2.2 and is held out again in 5.5 by a kneeling man; the box everybody calls poison is what lets her be buried and then get up.

techniques.name: The inventory
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.inThisBook: Iachimo recites the tapestry of Cleopatra, the chimneypiece of Dian bathing, the fretted roof and the two winking Cupids on the andirons. He admits none of it proves anything, and Posthumus is worn down by the sheer length of the list before the bracelet appears.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: A sung passage standing outside the dialogue, free to say what the speaking characters cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Two songs sit either side of the play's middle. Cloten pays for the lark at heaven's gate to wake a woman who loathes him, and the brothers speak, not sing, Fear no more over a sister they believe is a dead boy.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character built to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Cloten and Posthumus are the same build, want the same woman and end up in the same suit. In 4.1 Cloten measures his legs against his rival's and finds them better, and in 4.2 Imogen looks at the body and cannot tell them apart.

techniques.name: Prophecy
techniques.definition: A statement about the future that shapes the action by being believed, whether or not it is true.
techniques.inThisBook: Jupiter leaves a tablet about a lion's whelp and a lopped cedar on the sleeping Posthumus. It stays unreadable until a soothsayer takes apart Leo-natus and mollis aer in 5.5, by which time everything it promises has already happened.

techniques.name: The set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself.
techniques.inThisBook: The Leonati ghosts circle the prisoner in rhymed fourteeners and Jupiter descends on an eagle throwing a thunderbolt. Nothing in 5.4 moves the plot except the tablet he leaves behind, and the scene needs machinery in the theatre roof.

techniques.name: Recognition
techniques.definition: The moment a character's real identity or history becomes known, and the scene has to absorb the shock of it.
techniques.inThisBook: The last scene does this two dozen times over: the Queen's confession, the ring, the page who is a wife, the husband who strikes her, the headless man, the banished lord, the stolen princes and the mole on a neck, each landing before the one before it has been taken in.

quotations.text: It is a manacle of love; I'll place it Upon this fairest prisoner.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: Clasping the bracelet on Imogen's arm as they part, minutes before her father drives him out of Britain.
quotations.analysis: The love-token is named a fetter and the wife a prisoner in the same breath, and Posthumus means it as gallantry. The play takes him at his word instead: the bracelet is the thing that will be used against her, and the Queen has just called Imogen her prisoner in the scene's opening line.

quotations.text: O blessed that I might not! I chose an eagle, And did avoid a puttock.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Answering Cymbeline, who has just told her she could have married the Queen's son.
quotations.analysis: A puttock is a kite, the carrion hawk that will not hunt. Imogen answers a king in the middle of a rage with a falconer's joke, and picks the comparison that ranks men the way a court ranks birds. It is the first sign that she will argue rank on its own ground and win.

quotations.text: But I make my wager rather against your confidence than her reputation
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: In Philario's house in Rome, pressing Posthumus towards the bet after he has refused it once.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence that makes the wager possible. By shifting the target from Imogen to Posthumus's certainty, Iachimo lets him agree without admitting he is putting his wife up as a stake. He has found the exact form of words a proud man can accept, and Philario's attempt to call it off comes one line too late.

quotations.text: Our Tarquin thus Did softly press the rushes ere he waken'd The chastity he wounded.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Stepping out of the trunk into Imogen's bedchamber at midnight.
quotations.analysis: He compares himself to a rapist before he has done anything, and the comparison is his own idea. Shakespeare had written Tarquin's approach at length in The Rape of Lucrece, and the echo tells an audience exactly how to feel about a man who will in fact only look. The word our makes Rome the shared ancestor of both crimes.

quotations.text: Here's a voucher Stronger than ever law could make; this secret Will force him think I have pick'd the lock and ta'en The treasure of her honour.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Having found the mole under Imogen's breast, deciding he need write nothing else down.
quotations.analysis: A voucher is a document proving a title, and Iachimo knows he has manufactured one out of a birthmark. He says outright that it will force Posthumus to think, which is not the same as showing him anything true. The language of locks, treasure and forfeit runs all through his speech and turns a marriage into a property claim.

quotations.text: She hath been reading late The tale of Tereus; here the leaf's turn'd down Where Philomel gave up.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Noticing the book Imogen fell asleep over before he came out of the trunk.
quotations.analysis: Ovid's Philomel is raped by Tereus and has her tongue cut out so she cannot accuse him. Imogen has fallen asleep at the page where the victim stops speaking, and a man is standing over her bed collecting the evidence that will silence her. The detail is offered as one more item in an inventory, which is what makes it cold.

quotations.text: Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings, And Phœbus 'gins arise,
quotations.speaker: A Musician
quotations.context: The aubade Cloten has hired to be played at Imogen's door at first light.
quotations.analysis: One of the loveliest songs in Shakespeare is paid for by the nastiest man in the play, who has just told the musicians to try whether they can penetrate her with their fingering. The beauty is real and so is the purpose behind it, and the scene gives an audience no way of keeping them apart.

quotations.text: His mean'st garment That ever hath but clipp'd his body, is dearer In my respect, than all the hairs above thee
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Losing patience with Cloten at her chamber door, after he has called Posthumus a beggar bred on scraps.
quotations.analysis: It is the sharpest insult in the play and the most expensive. Cloten repeats the phrase four times in the next twenty lines, and two acts later he is wearing that garment in a Welsh wood, intending to kill its owner in it. Imogen will meet her own sentence again beside a headless body.

quotations.text: Could I find out The woman's part in me! For there's no motion That tends to vice in man but I affirm It is the woman's part.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: Alone in Rome, immediately after handing Iachimo the ring.
quotations.analysis: Having decided his wife is false, he works outward until every fault in the world belongs to women, including the faults in himself. The speech is a man building a general law out of one bad evening, and its logic is the same as the wager's: a single case is made to stand for all cases. He ends by resolving to write against them.

quotations.text: Britain is a world by itself, and we will nothing pay for wearing our own noses.
quotations.speaker: Cloten
quotations.context: Interrupting the Roman ambassador's demand for the tribute Cassibelan granted.
quotations.analysis: The play gives its most quotable statement of British independence to its greatest fool, and puts it in prose between two speeches of the Queen's ringing verse. The argument is not silly, which is the difficulty: Cymbeline acts on it, goes to war, wins, and then in the last scene quietly pays the money anyway.

quotations.text: How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature!
quotations.speaker: Belarius
quotations.context: Alone outside the cave, having just watched the two boys go up the mountain.
quotations.analysis: Belarius has spent twenty years raising princes as hunters and cannot keep the blood down. He goes on to describe Guiderius flushing and straining at a war story, acting out the feats in his sleep. The play backs him: the boys' courage in the lane wins the battle, and nobody has taught it to them.

quotations.text: 'tis slander, Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue Outvenoms all the worms of Nile
quotations.speaker: Pisanio
quotations.context: Watching Imogen read the letter that accuses her of adultery and orders her death.
quotations.analysis: Pisanio names the play's real weapon. Nobody in Cymbeline is killed by a lie's author; the lie travels by letter and post-horse from Rome to Wales and does its work at a distance. He has just said the paper cut her throat already, which leaves his sword with nothing to do and makes his disobedience possible.

quotations.text: Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion, And for I am richer than to hang by th' walls I must be ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Working out why her husband wants her dead, moments after reading the accusation.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for clothing, which is the play's currency for worth, and turns herself into a gown too good to be left hanging and so worth cutting up. The bitterness is in richer: being valuable is the reason for the destruction. Within two hundred lines she will be putting on a boy's doublet to stay alive.

quotations.text: I' th' world's volume Our Britain seems as of it, but not in't; In a great pool a swan's nest.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Told by Pisanio that if she cannot go back to court she cannot stay in Britain at all.
quotations.analysis: The book and the pool pull in opposite directions: Britain is a page bound into the world's volume but somehow not printed in it, and a nest at the centre of water that could swallow it. Imogen gets the play's most exact image of the island because she is the only character being forced to leave it.

quotations.text: You must forget to be a woman; change Command into obedience
quotations.speaker: Pisanio
quotations.context: Setting out what Imogen will have to do to pass as the page Fidele.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is a list of subtractions, and the first thing to go is the right to give orders. A princess must learn to be spoken to as a servant is spoken to, and Pisanio goes on to add gibes, sauciness and a sunburnt cheek. Imogen cuts him off to say she is almost a man already.

quotations.text: No, nor thy tailor, rascal, Who is thy grandfather; he made those clothes, Which, as it seems, make thee.
quotations.speaker: Guiderius
quotations.context: Answering Cloten, who has demanded whether Guiderius knows him by his clothes.
quotations.analysis: A boy raised in a cave punctures the whole court system of rank in one line, and does it by taking the question literally. Cloten is wearing Posthumus's suit, so the clothes really are making him something he is not. The joke is about to become a beheading, and then a burial that mistakes one man for another.

quotations.text: Our courtiers say all's savage but at court. Experience, O, thou disprov'st report!
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Alone at the mouth of the cave, sick, after the three hunters have gone out for the day.
quotations.analysis: She has been at court all her life and in a cave for two days, and the cave is winning. The couplet sets report against experience, which is the argument the whole play is having: Posthumus took a report over twenty years of experience and ordered a murder on it. Imogen is about to swallow the drug that will bury her.

quotations.text: Fear no more the heat o' th' sun, Nor the furious winter's rages … Golden lads and girls all must, As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.
quotations.speaker: Guiderius
quotations.context: The first stanza of the dirge, spoken and not sung, over a body the brothers believe is the boy Fidele.
quotations.analysis: The most famous lines in the play are spoken over a living woman by her own brothers, who do not know who she is, beside the corpse of the man who meant to rape her. Guiderius says he cannot sing and will word it instead, so the great song of the play arrives stripped of its music, in a flat voice, at a grave dug for nobody.

quotations.text: A headless man? The garments of Posthumus? I know the shape of's leg; this is his hand
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Waking from the drug beside Cloten's body, which is dressed in her husband's suit.
quotations.analysis: She identifies him by the leg, the hand, the thigh, the arms, and every single identification is correct about the clothes and wrong about the man. This is the wager repeated on her: accurate observation assembled into a false conclusion. The one part of the body that would have settled it is the part Guiderius threw in the creek.

quotations.text: The heaviness and guilt within my bosom Takes off my manhood. I have belied a lady, The Princess of this country
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Beaten and disarmed on the battlefield by a poor soldier he does not recognise as Posthumus.
quotations.analysis: Iachimo explains his own defeat as a physical effect of guilt, which is the only supernatural claim he ever makes. The play lets him be right: he loses to the husband he cheated, without either man knowing. Everything he says here he will say again, at greater length and unprompted, in the tent.

quotations.text: Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift, The more delay'd, delighted.
quotations.speaker: Jupiter
quotations.context: Descending on an eagle to silence the ghosts of the Leonati, who have been complaining about their son's treatment.
quotations.analysis: The god arrives to tell four ghosts that their suffering was never their business. It is the play's only direct statement of how it works, and it is unsatisfying on purpose: a divine plan that explains an ordered murder as a delay in the delivery of happiness. The audience has watched Imogen buried alive and is entitled to be unconvinced.

quotations.text: Kneel not to me. The pow'r that I have on you is to spare you; The malice towards you to forgive you.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: To Iachimo, who has knelt and offered back the ring and the bracelet.
quotations.analysis: A man who ordered his wife's murder on this man's word declines to take anything from him. The balance of the two lines, power against malice, spare against forgive, is the play's whole fifth act in miniature. Cymbeline immediately takes the cue and extends the pardon to the entire Roman army.

quotations.text: No, my lord; I have got two worlds by't.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Answering her father, who has just said that finding her brothers has cost her a kingdom.
quotations.analysis: Cymbeline counts in thrones and his daughter counts in brothers, and she has the better arithmetic. She has lost the succession and gained two men she already chose to love in a cave when she had no reason to. The line also quietly disposes of the one grievance that would have made the reunion political.

quotations.text: Although the victor, we submit to Cæsar And to the Roman empire, promising To pay our wonted tribute
quotations.speaker: Cymbeline
quotations.context: The peace settlement, after Britain has won the battle and taken Lucius prisoner.
quotations.analysis: Britain wins the war and pays the money, and the king blames the refusal on his dead wife. No Roman asks for this; it is offered. The play ends its imperial plot the way it ends its marriage plot, by handing back what was taken and calling the result peace, and the last word of the scene is exactly that.

timeline.label: Boccaccio finishes the Decameron
timeline.detail: The ninth tale of the second day has a merchant wager on his wife's chastity and a rival win it by being carried into her bedroom in a chest.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles, second edition
timeline.detail: Shakespeare takes Cymbeline, Cassibelan and the quarrel over the Roman tribute from the British books, and reorders the reigns to suit himself.

timeline.label: The King's Men take the Blackfriars
timeline.detail: An indoor playhouse with descent machinery in the roof, of the kind the Jupiter scene asks for.

timeline.label: Cymbeline written
timeline.detail: Composed alongside Pericles, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, at the end of Shakespeare's working life.

timeline.label: Simon Forman writes down what he saw
timeline.detail: His notebook records the wager, the man in the trunk and the cave in Wales. Forman died that September, so the play had been staged by then.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: No quarto survives. The Folio classes it as a tragedy and prints it last, closing the volume.

timeline.label: Played at court for Charles I
timeline.detail: The Master of the Revels recorded a performance by the King's players on New Year's Day, and noted that the king liked it.

timeline.label: D'Urfey rewrites it as The Injured Princess
timeline.detail: Thomas D'Urfey's version, subtitled The Fatal Wager, kept the stage in place of Shakespeare's text for the best part of a century.

timeline.label: Garrick brings the play back to Drury Lane
timeline.detail: David Garrick played Posthumus himself and returned something close to Shakespeare's text to the repertory.

timeline.label: Ellen Terry plays Imogen at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Henry Irving took Iachimo. Bernard Shaw reviewed it, praised Terry and attacked almost everything else in the play.

timeline.label: Shaw rewrites the last act
timeline.detail: Cymbeline Refinished replaces the cascade of recognitions with a short scene in which Imogen is markedly less pleased to have her husband back.

timeline.label: The RSC makes Cymbeline a queen
timeline.detail: Melly Still's production cast Gillian Bevan as a ruling queen and set the British scenes in a shut-in, decaying country.

places.name: Milford Haven
places.note: The Welsh port named in the forged letter. Imogen rides for it and never arrives; the Roman legions land there instead.

places.name: The Preseli Hills
places.note: The mountain country above the haven, where Belarius keeps his cave and the princes hunt for the pot.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Philario's house, where the wager is drawn up by lawyers and Posthumus is talked out of his marriage.

places.name: Lud's Town
places.note: The legendary name for London. Cloten swears he will set the brothers' heads on its gates, and the play ends marching there to ratify the peace.

places.name: The Blackfriars playhouse
places.note: The indoor theatre the King's Men had in hand by 1609, with the machinery to lower Jupiter and his eagle through the roof.

criticalViews.position: Johnson: the plot will not bear looking at
criticalViews.summary: Samuel Johnson listed the faults — names and manners from different centuries jumbled together, events impossible in any way of life — and concluded there was no point in criticising them at length. The complaint has stuck, and Cymbeline is still the Shakespeare play most often called a mess.
criticalViews.counter: Johnson was holding the play to a standard of probability it never claims. The last scene is built and timed as a set piece, and audiences who watch it performed laugh with it and gasp on cue; what reads on the page as carelessness works in a theatre as machinery.

criticalViews.summary: Grouped with Pericles, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, the play becomes a study in loss and repair: a family scattered, twenty years gone, a daughter thought dead, sons restored and a father forgiven more than he deserves.
criticalViews.counter: The grouping is a Victorian tidy-up. The Folio calls the play a tragedy and prints it among them, and the romance label smooths over what is actually on stage — a husband ordering his wife's murder, a rape planned in detail, and a head thrown into a stream.

criticalViews.summary: James I styled himself Emperor of Britain and sold his reign as a new Augustan peace. The play ends with a British and a Roman ensign carried side by side into Lud's Town, and it sends its heroine to Milford Haven, where Henry Tudor landed in 1485.
criticalViews.counter: The flattery does not hold up. Cymbeline wins the war and then agrees to pay the tribute he refused, which is an odd compliment to a king who disliked being told what he owed; and the Welsh scenes are pastoral throughout, with no interest in union or government at all.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Posthumus worth forgiving?
plan: Start with 1.5, where the ring is staked in public, in front of strangers, before Iachimo has done anything at all.
Track what actually convinces him in 2.4 — the room, then the bracelet, then the mole — and note that Philario names the obvious alternative and is brushed aside.
Read the murder order in 3.4 as Imogen reads it, and count how few lines it takes him to move from doubt to a written instruction.
Weigh 5.1 and 5.4: he asks to be hanged before he knows she is alive, which is the only version of his remorse that costs him anything.
Close on 5.5, where he strikes her once more before he knows her, and decide whether Hang there like fruit settles the account.

essayQuestions.question: What does Iachimo's night in the bedchamber actually prove?
plan: Set out exactly what he takes from the room in 2.2: pictures, chimneypiece, andirons, bracelet, mole, and the book left open at Philomel.
Show that every item is true and the inference from them is false, so the audience watches proof being manufactured out of facts.
Use Posthumus's own resistance in 2.4 — he dismisses the tapestry and the chimneypiece as hearsay — to identify which detail does the damage, and why.
Take Iachimo at his word on the voucher stronger than law, and ask what kind of court he imagines himself in.
Finish with 5.5, where the same man's unprompted speech undoes in fifty lines everything his evidence did in two acts.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the play send Imogen to Wales?
essayQuestions.focus: Court, cave and the nature of the princes
plan: Begin with what she is escaping in 3.4 and what Pisanio tells her she will have to stop being.
Read Belarius's opening speech in 3.3 on the low door and the arched gates of monarchs as the play's case for the cave.
Use her aside in 4.2 on courtiers, savagery and experience as the moment the case is tested and holds.
Turn to the brothers: their instinct for the fight in 5.2 and 5.3 is what Belarius calls the sparks of nature, and the battle proves him right.
End with what Wales costs her: Cloten's body, the drug, the grave and a Roman master, all inside one act.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of Cymbeline a happy one?
essayQuestions.focus: Recognition, pardon and the price of the peace
plan: Count the revelations in 5.5 and notice the order: the Queen's confession comes first, so the court learns it has been governed by somebody who hated it.
Sort the cast into the forgiven and the dead: Iachimo, Belarius, Guiderius and the whole Roman army are pardoned; Cloten and the Queen are not there to ask.
Set Imogen's two worlds against what she has lost — a husband who struck her in front of the court, and years she does not get back.
Examine the tribute: Britain wins, pays, and calls it peace. Decide whether that is generosity or a climb-down dressed up.
Weigh the closing line, with its bloody hands washed, against the dirge the brothers spoke over a grave in Act 4.

discussionQuestions: Iachimo tells Posthumus nothing but the truth and destroys a marriage with it. What is missing from his account, and why does nobody notice?
Pisanio disobeys a direct order from a master he loves. Was he right, and would he still have been right if Imogen had died on the road to Milford?
Cloten is a figure of fun for three acts and then plans a rape. Does the comedy make the threat worse, or blunt it?
Two boys raised in a cave behave like princes the moment a fight starts. Does the play convince you that breeding shows, or does it simply insist on it?
Imogen spends most of the play as a boy and is not called Imogen again until the last scene. What does she gain by being Fidele, and what does it cost her?
Britain wins the war and pays the tribute anyway. Is that an ending, or an evasion?

related.why: The other late play in which a husband decides his wife is false on no real evidence, and gets her back after years of being wrong.
Both plays run on a trusted outsider who builds a case out of a stolen token and a few accurate details.
A bride is slandered by a scene staged outside her window and then mourned as dead, which is the Imogen plot played for comedy.
The same late machinery of scattered families, long journeys and a daughter recovered from a supposed grave.
Written within a year or two of Cymbeline, and ending the same way: a ruler who pardons everyone and gives back what he has won.
